$schema_note: Single source of truth for TickerScope metrics. Backend uses `id` as the payload key and `source_key` to map yfinance info fields; frontend uses label/group/format for tiles and what/how_to_read/example_template for the explainer popover. Templates accept {ticker}, {value} (formatted) and {value_int} (rounded whole number, no unit).

metrics.label: Market cap
metrics.what: The total price tag the stock market puts on the whole company: share price times the number of shares.
metrics.how_to_read: Bigger means a larger, usually steadier company; under about $2B is 'small cap', over $200B is 'mega cap'. Size says nothing about whether the price is fair.
metrics.example_template: At today's price, buying every share of {ticker} would cost about {value}.

metrics.label: Enterprise value
metrics.what: What it would cost to buy the whole business outright: market cap plus its debt, minus the cash it already has.
metrics.how_to_read: Compare it to market cap: if EV is much higher the company carries a lot of debt; if EV is lower it is sitting on more cash than debt.
metrics.example_template: Taking on {ticker}'s debt and pocketing its cash, the whole business is worth about {value}.

metrics.label: 52-week low / high
metrics.what: The lowest and highest prices the stock traded at over the past year, with a bar showing where today's price sits between them.
metrics.how_to_read: Near the high means the stock has been strong lately; near the low means it has been beaten down. Neither is a signal on its own.
metrics.example_template: Over the last year {ticker} traded between {value}.

metrics.label: Avg volume (3 mo)
metrics.what: How many shares change hands on a typical day, averaged over the last three months.
metrics.how_to_read: Higher volume means it is easy to buy or sell without moving the price. Very low volume (under a few hundred thousand) can mean wide spreads and jumpy prices.
metrics.example_template: About {value} shares of {ticker} trade on an average day.

metrics.label: Beta
metrics.what: How much the stock tends to move compared with the overall market (the S&P 500 counts as 1.0).
metrics.how_to_read: Above 1 swings more than the market, below 1 swings less; around 1 moves with it. Higher beta means bumpier rides both up and down.
metrics.example_template: With a beta of {value}, if the market moves 1% then {ticker} has tended to move about {value}%.

metrics.label: Shares outstanding
metrics.what: The total number of shares that exist right now, held by everyone from founders to index funds.
metrics.how_to_read: Watch the trend rather than the number: falling means the company is buying back stock (good for owners), rising means it is issuing more and diluting each share.
metrics.example_template: {ticker} is split into about {value} shares.

metrics.label: P/E (TTM)
metrics.what: Price-to-earnings: the share price divided by the profit per share earned over the last twelve months (TTM).
metrics.how_to_read: Roughly, how many years of current profit you are paying for. Under ~15 is cheap-ish, 20–30 is typical for a growing company, above 40 means investors expect fast growth. Negative or blank means the company lost money.
metrics.example_template: {ticker}'s P/E of {value} means you pay about ${value_int} for every $1 of the last year's profit.

metrics.label: Forward P/E
metrics.what: Same idea as P/E, but using analysts' estimate of next year's profit per share instead of last year's.
metrics.how_to_read: Lower than the trailing P/E means profits are expected to grow; higher means they are expected to shrink. It rests on forecasts, so treat it as an educated guess.
metrics.example_template: Based on what analysts expect {ticker} to earn next year, you are paying about ${value_int} for every $1 of profit ({value}).

metrics.label: PEG
metrics.what: The P/E ratio divided by the expected yearly earnings growth rate. It asks whether the price is high because the company is growing fast.
metrics.how_to_read: Around 1 is often called fair; well under 1 can mean the growth is cheap; over 2 means you are paying a lot for that growth. Not meaningful when growth is negative.
metrics.example_template: {ticker}'s PEG of {value} sets its P/E against its expected growth; near 1 would be considered fairly priced for that growth.

metrics.label: Price/Sales (TTM)
metrics.what: Market cap divided by the last twelve months of revenue (sales). Useful for companies that are not yet profitable.
metrics.how_to_read: Under 2 is modest, 5–10 is rich, over 10 means investors are paying up for growth or very high margins. Compare within the same industry.
metrics.example_template: Investors are paying about ${value_int} for every $1 of yearly sales at {ticker} ({value}).

metrics.label: Price/Book
metrics.what: Market cap divided by book value (what the accountants say the company's assets minus debts are worth).
metrics.how_to_read: Near 1 means you pay about what the assets are worth on paper; banks and industrials often sit near 1–2, software and brands can be 10+ because their value is not on the balance sheet.
metrics.example_template: {ticker} trades at {value} its accounting book value.

metrics.label: EV/EBITDA
metrics.what: Enterprise value divided by EBITDA (earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization). A P/E-style ratio that ignores debt structure and accounting charges.
metrics.how_to_read: Under ~10 is generally cheap, 10–20 is normal, above 25 is expensive. Analysts like it for comparing companies with different debt levels.
metrics.example_template: Buying all of {ticker} would cost about {value_int} years of its current EBITDA ({value}).

metrics.label: EV/Revenue
metrics.what: Enterprise value divided by the last twelve months of revenue. Like Price/Sales but counting debt and cash too.
metrics.how_to_read: Under 2 is modest, above 10 is a premium usually reserved for fast growers with high margins.
metrics.example_template: The whole {ticker} business is valued at about {value} its yearly revenue.

metrics.label: Revenue (TTM)
metrics.what: Total sales over the trailing twelve months, before any costs are taken out. Also called the top line.
metrics.how_to_read: The raw size of the business. What matters more is whether it is growing and how much of it turns into profit (see the margins).
metrics.example_template: {ticker} brought in about {value} in sales over the last twelve months.

metrics.label: Revenue growth (YoY)
metrics.what: How much revenue changed compared with the same period a year earlier (year over year).
metrics.how_to_read: Positive is growing, negative is shrinking. Single digits is mature, 15–30% is fast, above 40% is rare and usually gets a rich valuation.
metrics.example_template: {ticker}'s sales changed {value} versus the same period a year ago.

metrics.label: Gross margin
metrics.what: The share of each sales dollar left after paying only the direct cost of making the product or delivering the service.
metrics.how_to_read: Higher is better and it depends heavily on the industry: software is often 70%+, retailers and grocers can be under 30%.
metrics.example_template: Of every $100 {ticker} sells, about ${value_int} is left after the direct cost of what it sold ({value}).

metrics.label: Operating margin
metrics.what: The share of each sales dollar left after all the costs of running the business (staff, rent, marketing, research), but before interest and taxes.
metrics.how_to_read: Higher is better; above 20% is strong, under 5% is thin, negative means the core business loses money.
metrics.example_template: {ticker} keeps about ${value_int} of every $100 in sales as operating profit ({value}).

metrics.label: Net margin
metrics.what: The share of each sales dollar that ends up as final profit after every cost, including interest and taxes. Also called the bottom line.
metrics.how_to_read: Higher is better; 10% is solid for most industries, 20%+ is excellent, negative means a net loss.
metrics.example_template: Out of every $100 in sales, {ticker} ended up with about ${value_int} in profit ({value}).

metrics.label: EBITDA (TTM)
metrics.what: Earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization over the last twelve months. A rough measure of the cash the operations throw off, ignoring financing and accounting charges.
metrics.how_to_read: Bigger is better and it should grow with revenue. It flatters companies with heavy equipment costs, so pair it with free cash flow.
metrics.example_template: {ticker}'s operations produced about {value} of EBITDA in the last twelve months.

metrics.label: Net income (TTM)
metrics.what: The final profit over the last twelve months after every expense, interest and tax. The dollar amount behind 'net margin'.
metrics.how_to_read: Positive and growing is what you want. A negative number is a loss. One-time items can swing it, so check a few years, not one.
metrics.example_template: {ticker} earned about {value} in profit over the last twelve months.

metrics.label: EPS (TTM)
metrics.what: Earnings per share: the last twelve months of profit divided by the number of shares. Your slice of the profit for each share you own.
metrics.how_to_read: Growing EPS is the main thing that pushes a stock up over time. Compare it with the share price to get the P/E ratio.
metrics.example_template: Each share of {ticker} earned {value} of profit over the last twelve months.

metrics.label: Forward EPS
metrics.what: Analysts' average estimate of profit per share for the next twelve months.
metrics.how_to_read: Higher than the trailing EPS means growth is expected. It is a forecast, and forecasts get revised.
metrics.example_template: Analysts expect each share of {ticker} to earn about {value} next year.

metrics.label: ROE
metrics.what: Return on equity: yearly profit as a percentage of the money shareholders have in the company (book value).
metrics.how_to_read: Higher is better; 15%+ is good, 25%+ is excellent. Very high ROE can also come from heavy borrowing, so glance at Debt/Equity too.
metrics.example_template: For every $100 of shareholder money in {ticker}, the company earned about ${value_int} this year ({value}).

metrics.label: ROA
metrics.what: Return on assets: yearly profit as a percentage of everything the company owns (factories, cash, inventory, and so on).
metrics.how_to_read: Higher means the company squeezes more profit out of what it owns. 5%+ is decent, 10%+ is strong; banks are naturally low (~1%) because they hold huge assets.
metrics.example_template: {ticker} earned about {value} on everything it owns over the past year.

metrics.label: Operating cash flow (TTM)
metrics.what: The actual cash the day-to-day business generated over the last twelve months, before spending on equipment or paying investors.
metrics.how_to_read: Positive and roughly in line with (or above) net income is healthy. If profit is high but cash flow is low, the profit may be on paper only.
metrics.example_template: {ticker}'s regular operations generated about {value} in cash over the last twelve months.

metrics.label: Free cash flow (TTM)
metrics.what: Operating cash flow minus what the company spent on buildings and equipment. The cash truly left over for dividends, buybacks, paying down debt, or acquisitions.
metrics.how_to_read: Many investors call this the real profit. Positive and growing is what you want; negative means the company is burning cash.
metrics.example_template: After paying for its equipment, {ticker} had about {value} of cash left over in the last twelve months.

metrics.label: FCF yield
metrics.what: Free cash flow divided by market cap: the cash return you would get on the price you pay, if the company handed all of it to shareholders.
metrics.how_to_read: Higher is cheaper. Under 2% is pricey, 4–6% is reasonable, above 8% is cheap or the market doubts the cash will keep coming.
metrics.example_template: At today's price, {ticker} generates about {value} of its market value in free cash each year.

metrics.label: Total cash
metrics.what: Cash and near-cash investments the company has on hand right now.
metrics.how_to_read: More is a cushion for tough times and for deals. Compare it with total debt to see if the company is a net borrower or a net saver.
metrics.example_template: {ticker} is holding about {value} in cash and short-term investments.

metrics.label: Total debt
metrics.what: Everything the company has borrowed, short-term and long-term, including leases.
metrics.how_to_read: Debt is not bad by itself; the question is whether cash flow covers the interest comfortably. Set it next to total cash and EBITDA.
metrics.example_template: {ticker} owes about {value} to lenders.

metrics.label: Debt/Equity
metrics.what: Total debt divided by shareholders' equity (book value). How much the company relies on borrowing versus owners' money.
metrics.how_to_read: Under 0.5× is conservative, 1–2× is common, above 3× is heavily leveraged. Utilities and banks run high by design; tech companies usually run low.
metrics.example_template: For every $1 of shareholder money in {ticker}, the company has borrowed about ${value_int} ({value}).

metrics.label: Current ratio
metrics.what: Short-term assets (cash, receivables, inventory) divided by short-term bills due within a year. A quick check on whether the company can pay what it owes soon.
metrics.how_to_read: Above 1 means it can cover its near-term bills; 1.5–3 is comfortable; well below 1 can be a warning sign, though some fast-turnover businesses live fine below 1.
metrics.example_template: {ticker} has about ${value_int} of short-term assets for every $1 of bills due this year ({value}).

metrics.label: Dividend yield
metrics.what: The yearly cash dividend per share as a percentage of the current share price.
metrics.how_to_read: The income you would earn just by holding. 1–3% is typical for a payer, 5%+ is high and can mean the market doubts the payout will last. Blank means no dividend.
metrics.example_template: Holding {ticker} pays you about {value} of its price in dividends each year.

metrics.label: Payout ratio
metrics.what: The share of profit that gets paid out as dividends.
metrics.how_to_read: Under 60% leaves room to keep paying and growing the dividend; above 100% means the company is paying out more than it earns, which usually cannot last.
metrics.example_template: {ticker} pays out about {value} of its profit as dividends.

metrics.label: Next earnings date
metrics.what: The next day the company is scheduled to report its quarterly results.
metrics.how_to_read: Stocks often move sharply on this day. If you are about to buy or sell, it is worth knowing whether earnings are tomorrow or two months away.
metrics.example_template: {ticker} is next scheduled to report results on {value}.

metrics.label: Ex-dividend date
metrics.what: The cutoff day for the next dividend: you must own the shares before this date to receive it.
metrics.how_to_read: Buy on or after this date and you miss the upcoming payment. The price usually dips by about the dividend amount that morning.
metrics.example_template: To collect {ticker}'s next dividend you needed to own it before {value}.
